findings.claim: Nepal's earthquake was much larger (7.8 vs 6.3 - about a hundred times more energy released)
findings.truth: A 1.5 difference in moment magnitude is 10^(1.5x1.5) = about 178 times the energy. 'About 180 times' is right; 100 matches neither the energy ratio nor the amplitude ratio (about 32).
findings.evidence: recomputation from the magnitude-energy relation

findings.claim: Nepal's death toll was around fifty times larger, despite a population that is only about five times larger than Christchurch's
findings.truth: Nepal's population is about 28 million and Christchurch's about 380,000 - roughly 75 times, not five. The comparison as written also destroys the argument it is making, so the false clause is replaced with a true one about building quality.
findings.evidence: recomputation from published population figures

findings.claim: 185 people died, around half in the collapse of a single six-storey building (the CTV building)
findings.truth: The lesson's own collapsible states 115 of the 185 died in the CTV building - nearly two thirds. The knowledge check repeated 'around half'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction; CTV Royal Commission figure of 115

findings.claim: Examiners want named statistics in case-study answers.
findings.truth: An unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour. Rewritten as advice in the house voice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: 'there is a 60% chance of a magnitude 6+ earthquake in the San Francisco Bay Area in the next 30 years'
findings.truth: The published USGS UCERF3 forecast is a 72% chance of a magnitude 6.7 or larger earthquake in the Bay Area within 30 years. A magnitude 6+ probability would be higher still, so 60% is wrong either way.
findings.evidence: USGS UCERF3 (Wikipedia summary: 52 / 72 / 94%)

findings.claim: KC2: 'Which is the only one of the four Ps that does NOT depend on advance warning?' keyed to Protection
findings.truth: Planning (drills, hazard maps, evacuation routes) also needs no advance warning, so a student choosing Planning was marked wrong. The question is rewritten to key uniquely to Planning.
findings.evidence: internal logic of the lesson's own definitions

findings.claim: hurricanes appear at 10-30 degrees north or south
findings.truth: The lesson teaches 5-30 degrees in the main text and the conclusion. The collapsible contradicted it.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction; AQA spec range

findings.claim: Examiners want the formation conditions stated in order
findings.truth: Unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: parts of New Orleans were dark for over a month
findings.truth: Most of New Orleans had power restored within about 10 days; the month-long outages were in coastal Louisiana parishes.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Hurricane Ida (power restoration section)

findings.claim: Cumbria had already flooded in 2009 (Storm Cockermouth)
findings.truth: There was no 'Storm Cockermouth'. UK storm naming began in 2015 with Abigail. Cockermouth is the town badly flooded in the November 2009 Cumbria floods.
findings.evidence: Met Office storm-naming scheme start date (2015-16)

findings.field: content_html + conclusion + L19 content_html + L19 practice_questions
findings.claim: climate change raised Storm Desmond's rainfall totals by an estimated 40%
findings.truth: The Met Office attribution study found the event was made about 40% MORE LIKELY by human-driven warming. It did not find the rainfall was 40% heavier. Classic attribution misreading, repeated in L19 and in an L19 model answer.
findings.evidence: Met Office rapid attribution of Storm Desmond, December 2015

findings.field: content_html + conclusion + flashcards + practice; also L19, L20
findings.claim: The Met Office records show: 9 of the 10 wettest years on record have happened since 2000; storm names ran out for the first time in 2015-16; floods costing more than 100 million pounds happen roughly twice as often as in the 1980s
findings.truth: None of the three is a Met Office finding. Storm names have never been exhausted (the first 2015-16 season used 11 names, Abigail to Katie). Replaced with figures the Met Office does publish: the winter half-year for 2016-2025 was 13% wetter than 1961-1990, and 2025 was the warmest year in the UK series from 1884. The fabricated statistic also appeared in L19 (content + flashcard), L20 (content) and two model answers.
findings.evidence: Met Office State of the UK Climate page (fetched 6 Sep 2026)

findings.claim: The summer of 2022 was the driest since 1976; reservoirs fell to 50%
findings.truth: The 'since 1976' comparison applies to the first eight months of the year, not the summer. The settled records are: July 2022 was the driest July in England since 1935, and reservoir levels reached a 25-year low.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 2022 United Kingdom drought

findings.claim: Bridges in Carlisle, Cockermouth and Pooley Bridge collapsed
findings.truth: Pooley Bridge (standing since 1764) was washed away; the only other recorded collapse was a bridge on the Isle of Man. No bridge collapse at Carlisle or Cockermouth is recorded for Desmond.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Storm Desmond

findings.claim: For UK weather hazard case-study questions, examiners want named places and figures
findings.truth: Unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The yew tree of the Amazon produced taxol, used to treat cancer.
findings.truth: Taxol (paclitaxel) comes from the Pacific yew, Taxus brevifolia, a temperate North American conifer. There is no Amazon yew. Replaced with a true rainforest medicine: quinine from the cinchona tree of South America.
findings.evidence: settled pharmacology of paclitaxel

findings.claim: Jaguars are the only big cat that hunts mainly in water.
findings.truth: Jaguars hunt mainly on land (peccary, capybara, deer) though they swim well and take caiman in water; tigers also hunt in water. 'Only big cat that hunts mainly in water' is false twice over.
findings.evidence: settled zoology

findings.claim: Around 17% of the Amazon has been cleared ... The total area lost is now about the size of France.
findings.truth: 17% of 5.5 million km2 is about 935,000 km2. France is 552,000 km2; France plus Germany is about 910,000 km2.
findings.evidence: recomputation from the lesson's own figures

findings.claim: Around 12 million hectares of land are lost to desertification every year - an area larger than England.
findings.truth: 12 million hectares is 120,000 km2. England is 130,279 km2, so the annual loss is slightly SMALLER than England, not larger.
findings.evidence: recomputation; ONS area of England

findings.claim: the Great Green Wall: a 7,000km belt of trees
findings.truth: The planned wall is 7,775 km, published by the initiative as nearly 8,000 km.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Great Green Wall (Africa)

findings.claim: Sand is dropped first as it is finest; pebbles and shingle are dropped where wave energy is higher.
findings.truth: Deposition works the other way: the heaviest material drops first as energy falls, and the finest material is carried furthest and settles in the calmest water. As written the two clauses also contradict each other.
findings.evidence: settled coastal process; internal contradiction

findings.claim: the long shingle ridge of Chesil Beach - an 18 km bar
findings.truth: Chesil Beach is 29 km (18 miles) long. The mile figure had been relabelled as kilometres.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Chesil Beach: 'a length of 29 kilometres (18 mi)'

findings.claim: Examiners look for the chain of cause and effect ... A stage with the wrong example loses marks
findings.truth: Unverifiable examiner claim plus an invented mark-scheme rule.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner and mark-scheme claims

findings.claim: For 9-mark 'Assess' questions on coastal management, examiners want a balanced argument
findings.truth: Unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Rivers erode in four ways - the same processes that operate at the coast, plus one more.
findings.truth: The four listed (hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution) are exactly the four taught for the coast in lesson 14. There is no extra process.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 14

findings.claim: The cross profile looks at the river from the side, slicing across the valley.
findings.truth: The side-on view is the LONG profile, defined two paragraphs earlier. The cross profile is the view across the valley. The sentence conflated the two.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction

findings.claim: KC3 fill: 'An _______ lake forms when a meander is cut off' with options oxbow / ox-bow / ox-pond / ox-flood, keyed to ox-bow
findings.truth: 'Oxbow' and 'ox-bow' are both correct spellings, so a student choosing the first option was marked wrong for a right answer. The distractor is replaced with 'ox-loop'.
findings.evidence: standard English spelling of oxbow lake

findings.claim: Examiners expect you to know one named UK example ... Examiners reward sequential logic over a list of features.
findings.truth: Unverifiable claims about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The Environment Agency issues colour-coded warnings (yellow / amber / red)
findings.truth: Yellow, amber and red are Met Office WEATHER warnings. Environment Agency flood warnings have three named levels: flood alert, flood warning and severe flood warning. A student writing 'yellow flood warning' would be wrong.
findings.evidence: Environment Agency flood warning service levels

findings.claim: caribou calves are being born before the peak grass growth they depend on
findings.truth: The documented Arctic trophic mismatch runs the other way: plant emergence has advanced with warming while calving timing has not, so calves now arrive AFTER the forage peak.
findings.evidence: Post and Forchhammer, Greenland caribou trophic mismatch

findings.claim: the polar bear has hollow, transparent guard hairs that channel heat towards its black skin
findings.truth: The 'light pipe' or heat-channelling explanation was disproved (Koon 1998). The hairs are hollow and translucent and insulate by trapping air; the black skin absorbs the sunlight that reaches it.
findings.evidence: settled physics of polar bear pelage

findings.claim: The word 'interdependent' signals the examiner wants you to show the connections
findings.truth: Unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Windermere in the Lake District is the UK's longest lake (18 km) ... The UK's longest ribbon lake is Windermere
findings.truth: Loch Awe (41 km) and Loch Ness (36 km) are both longer. Windermere is England's longest lake, not the UK's.
findings.evidence: published lake lengths

findings.claim: Examiners reward accurate process terminology
findings.truth: Unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The Lake District became England's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017
findings.truth: Durham Castle and Cathedral, Stonehenge, Ironbridge Gorge, Fountains Abbey and the Giant's Causeway were all inscribed in 1986. The Lake District (2017) was England's newest at the time, not its first. The same claim appears in lesson 25.
findings.evidence: UNESCO World Heritage List inscription dates

findings.claim: Red Tarn corrie sits at 720 m below Helvellyn's eastern face, its backwall rising over 300 m
findings.truth: Helvellyn is 950 m and Red Tarn sits at about 718 m, so the backwall is about 230 m.
findings.evidence: recomputation from the lesson's own figure and Helvellyn's height

findings.claim: Examiners reward specific place names and the link between process and landform
findings.truth: Unverifiable claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Christchurch 2011: '$40 billion damage', set beside Nepal's '$7 billion'
findings.truth: NZ$40 billion is the New Zealand Treasury rebuild estimate, about US$28 billion. Nepal's $7 billion is US dollars, so the two case-study figures are not like for like. Options: (a) relabel as 'NZ$40 billion (about US$28 billion)' in all three places; (b) switch to the US$28 billion figure throughout; (c) leave, since no student would be marked wrong. Recommendation: (a) - one word per occurrence, and it makes the comparison honest.
findings.evidence: NZ Treasury rebuild estimate
findings.ruling: Leave: textbook figure or unsourced replacement.

findings.field: content_html (also lesson 16 and two mark schemes)
findings.claim: longshore drift moves sediment south along Holderness 'at around 1.5 metres per day'
findings.truth: No published source for this rate was found; Holderness transport is normally quoted as a sediment volume (about 500,000 tonnes a year), not a speed. The figure is presented as a memorisable exam number in two lessons and two model answers. Options: (a) delete the rate and keep 'steadily southwards'; (b) replace with the tonnage figure; (c) keep pending a source. Recommendation: (b) - the tonnage is publishable and does the same teaching job.
findings.evidence: no source found in this session
findings.ruling: Leave: textbook figure or unsourced replacement.

findings.claim: Lake District tourism: around 18 million visitors, about 2.4 billion pounds, around 16,000 jobs
findings.truth: Cumbria Tourism / STEAM figures usually quoted for the National Park are about 18-19 million visitors, 1.4 billion pounds of visitor spend and about 18,000 jobs; the 2.4 billion / 16,000 pairing could not be sourced. Options: (a) re-cite from the current STEAM report; (b) leave until the next narration pass. Recommendation: (a) before the lesson is re-narrated, since the figures are repeated in four fields.
findings.evidence: no source found in this session
findings.ruling: Leave: textbook figure or unsourced replacement.

findings.claim: Around 9,000 people were killed and 23,000 injured (Nepal 2015)
findings.truth: Official Nepalese figures give about 22,000 injured (22,309). The death toll is right. Not corrected because the difference is within reporting noise and not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: Nepal government casualty figures

findings.claim: New York City changed its rules: basement flats now require flood-proofing if they are to be legally rented out
findings.truth: New York's post-Ida response was the Rainfall Ready NYC plan plus a basement-apartment conversion pilot; a blanket legal requirement of this kind could not be verified. Left alone rather than replaced with a guess.
findings.evidence: not verified

findings.claim: Two people died directly. Total economic cost was estimated at over 500 million pounds.
findings.truth: Wikipedia records 3 deaths for Storm Desmond and damage of at least 870 million pounds. 'Over 500 million' is not false, and 'died directly' may be a defensible subset, so neither was edited.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Storm Desmond

findings.claim: Farming: with irrigation, even desert can produce crops - the Murray-Darling basin is a textbook example.
findings.truth: The Murray-Darling basin is semi-arid farmland in south-eastern Australia, roughly 2,000 km from the Western Desert case study, and is not a hot desert. A weak example rather than a wrong fact.
findings.evidence: physical geography of the Murray-Darling basin

findings.claim: By 2024, only around 18% of the planned area had been restored (Great Green Wall)
findings.truth: Published progress estimates vary widely: about 4% (UNCCD 2020 status report) to about 30% (2024 estimate, 30 million of 100 million hectares). The lesson's 18% sits between them and is defensible, so it was left.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Great Green Wall (Africa)

findings.claim: Permanent flood walls at Shrewsbury's Frankwell area - a 200 m sloping concrete wall
findings.truth: The Frankwell scheme is normally described as demountable barriers mounted on a permanent base wall, not a purely permanent wall. Not corrected without a source.
findings.evidence: not verified

findings.claim: Norber erratics: perched on limestone pedestals up to 50 cm high; the ice carried them uphill from the south
findings.truth: Wikipedia gives pedestals up to 30 cm. The source outcrop in Crummack Dale lies to the north of Norber, so 'from the south' is probably the wrong direction, but the article does not state the ice direction, so nothing was changed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Norber erratics

findings.claim: Lesson descriptions on lessons 17, 23, 24 and 25 are 101 characters
findings.truth: One character over the 100-character validator limit. Pre-existing and untouched by these edits; flagged in case the applier validates whole rows.
findings.evidence: character count

summary: 25 lessons read line by line against the AQA geography spec (sections 3.1.1-3.1.3 and the assessment section) and against published figures. 48 findings: 1 HIGH, 19 MEDIUM, 28 LOW; 37 are FIX (61 edits across 19 lessons), 3 ADJUDICATE, 8 NOTE. The heaviest problems are a fabricated Met Office statistic repeated in three lessons, an attribution error on Storm Desmond, an invented 'Storm Cockermouth', a taxol/Amazon-yew fabrication, Chesil Beach given in miles labelled as kilometres, a reversed deposition rule, a reversed Arctic trophic mismatch, two knowledge checks that marked correct answers wrong, and 'England's first UNESCO World Heritage Site' twice. No exam-structure errors were found: paper timing, marks, sections and question types are not asserted anywhere, and every practice question uses AQA-compatible mark tariffs. Ten unverifiable 'examiners want/reward' claims were rewritten in the house voice.
